features.citation: Jensen R. Cephalalgia 1999. Pericranial muscle tenderness (manual palpation) present in 70–90% of TTH; most pronounced in suboccipital, trapezius, and temporalis muscles.
ICHD-3 2018. TTH pain is bilateral in >90% of episodes; fronto-occipital 'hatband' distribution is the most characteristic radiation pattern. Unilateral onset alone makes TTH diagnosis uncertain.

features.evidenceLabel: Mild to moderate pain intensity (3–6/10) — TTH rarely severe
features.citation: Stovner LJ et al. Cephalalgia 2007. TTH intensity mild-moderate in >90% of episodes; severity ≥7/10 shifts probability towards migraine or secondary headache. Most patients maintain normal function.

features.evidenceLabel: Duration 30 minutes to 7 days (ICHD-3 criterion for episodic TTH)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Episodic TTH: 30 min–7 days duration. Chronic TTH: ≥15 days/month for >3 months. Duration <30 min is unusual for TTH and should prompt consideration of TACs.

features.evidenceLabel: Poor posture / prolonged desk or screen work exacerbates headache
features.citation: Fernández-de-las-Peñas C et al. Cephalalgia 2006. Sustained neck flexion (screen work, reading) increases myofascial trigger point activity in upper trapezius and suboccipitals. Common occupational TTH trigger.

features.evidenceLabel: Sleep deprivation or poor sleep quality as a precipitant
features.citation: Boardman HF et al. BMJ 2005. Poor sleep is the most commonly reported trigger in TTH (56% in population study); bidirectional relationship — headache also disrupts sleep.

features.evidenceLabel: Eye strain / uncorrected refractive error contributing to frontal headache
features.citation: Gil-Gouveia R & Martins IP. Headache 2002. Asthenopia (eye strain) and uncorrected refractive error can trigger or worsen TTH via frontal / periorbital muscle tension. Consider ophthalmology referral.

features.evidenceLabel: Pericranial muscle tenderness on manual palpation (frontal, temporalis, masseter, trapezius)
features.citation: Jensen R et al. Cephalalgia 1998. Pericranial muscle tenderness score (Total Tenderness Score) is the most important examination finding; TTS correlates with TTH frequency and intensity. LR+ 7.2.

features.evidenceLabel: Chronic daily headache (≥15 days/month) — chronic TTH pattern
features.citation: Scher AI et al. Headache 2003. Chronic TTH affects 2–3% of population; 80% of chronic daily headache in general practice. Medication overuse must be excluded when analgesic use >15 days/month (MOH).

features.evidenceLabel: Analgesic / triptan overuse (>10–15 days/month) — medication overuse headache
features.citation: Diener HC et al. Lancet Neurol 2019. Medication overuse headache (MOH) transforms episodic TTH/migraine into chronic daily headache. Simple analgesia >15d/month, triptans >10d/month are thresholds.

features.evidenceLabel: Comorbid anxiety or depression — bidirectional association with TTH
features.citation: Breslau N et al. Neurology 2000. Anxiety (OR 2.4) and depression (OR 2.2) strongly comorbid with TTH; central sensitisation and shared neurobiological pathways. Treat psychiatric comorbidity alongside headache.

features.evidenceLabel: Relief with NSAIDs (ibuprofen, aspirin) or paracetamol
features.citation: Bendtsen L et al. Eur J Neurol 2010. NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400–800mg) provide significant relief in acute TTH; NNT ~4. Combination analgesics (aspirin + caffeine) more effective but higher MOH risk.

features.evidenceLabel: Relief from massage, heat application, or relaxation techniques
features.citation: Nestoriuc Y et al. Cephalalgia 2008. Relaxation training and EMG biofeedback reduce TTH frequency 50% (meta-analysis NNT 3). Hot compress to neck and shoulders provides acute symptomatic relief.

features.evidenceLabel: Strictly unilateral onset — argues against TTH, suggests migraine or TAC
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. TTH is bilateral by definition; strictly unilateral onset is an exclusion criterion for TTH. Unilateral headache shifts diagnosis to migraine without aura or TACs.

features.evidenceLabel: Pulsating / throbbing quality — argues against TTH (ICHD-3 exclusion criterion)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Pulsating quality is an exclusion criterion for TTH and a positive criterion for migraine. Bilateral pressing/tightening distinguishes TTH from migraine at the character level alone.

features.evidenceLabel: Vomiting — strongly argues against TTH (not a feature of TTH)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Vomiting is an exclusion criterion for TTH. Its presence mandates reconsideration of migraine, SAH, raised ICP, or other secondary causes. TTH may very rarely cause mild nausea.

features.evidenceLabel: Thunderclap onset — excludes TTH; mandates SAH / RCVS / CVST exclusion
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. TTH is never thunderclap in onset. Sudden severe headache is explicitly listed as a red flag requiring neuroimaging regardless of subsequent TTH-like features.

features.evidenceLabel: Duration <30 minutes — too brief for TTH; consider TAC (cluster, SUNCT, SUNA)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Minimum TTH duration is 30 minutes. Attacks lasting 15–180 min with autonomic features = cluster headache; 1–600 sec = SUNCT/SUNA. Duration <30 min requires TAC workup.

features.evidenceLabel: Marked photophobia AND phonophobia together — argues for migraine over TTH
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. TTH permits only mild photophobia OR mild phonophobia (not both simultaneously). Both present simultaneously and marked = migraine criterion.

features.evidenceLabel: Palpable myofascial trigger points in suboccipital / trapezius / SCM muscles
features.citation: Fernandez-de-Las-Penas C et al. Headache 2007. Active myofascial trigger points in suboccipital, upper trapezius, and SCM muscles are found in >80% of patients with chronic TTH vs <20% of healthy controls (LR+ ~4.5). Trigger point pressure reproduction of the headache pattern strongly supports musculoskeletal origin.

features.evidenceLabel: Subjective neck and shoulder muscle tightness / stiffness associated with headache onset
features.citation: Jensen R. Cephalalgia 1999. Pericranial and cervical muscle tenderness is the most consistent finding in TTH, present in 86% of chronic and 72% of episodic TTH patients. Patients typically describe subjective tightness in the neck, shoulders, and scalp as part of the headache complex.

features.evidenceLabel: Jaw clenching, teeth grinding (bruxism), or temporomandibular joint tension associated with headache
features.citation: Svensson P & Graven-Nielsen T. Headache 2001. Bruxism and temporomandibular disorders (TMD) are strongly comorbid with TTH; masseter and temporalis muscle hyperactivity from nocturnal bruxism generates pericranial tenderness that directly triggers TTH. TMD is present in up to 40% of chronic TTH patients.

features.evidenceLabel: Caffeine withdrawal headache — missed dose in regular consumer; bilateral pressing, resolves with caffeine
features.citation: Silverman K et al. NEJM 1992. Caffeine withdrawal headache occurs in ~50% of regular caffeine consumers when intake is missed; clinically indistinguishable from episodic TTH (bilateral, pressing, mild-moderate). Resolves within 30–60 min of caffeine consumption. A daily caffeine habit followed by a weekend or illness-related miss is the classic scenario.

features.evidenceLabel: Fasting or skipped meals as a precipitant — hypoglycaemia-mediated vasodilation
features.citation: Blau JN & Thavapalan M. Headache 1988. Fasting or skipped meals precipitate headache in ~50% of headache clinic patients. The mechanism involves hypoglycaemia-mediated vasodilation and cortisol/adrenaline release. TTH is the most common headache phenotype triggered by fasting; prompt relief with eating is characteristic.

features.evidenceLabel: Inadequate hydration / dehydration as a recognised precipitant
features.citation: Blau JN. Cephalalgia 2005. Dehydration is a well-recognised precipitant of TTH; the proposed mechanism involves plasma hyperosmolarity triggering hypothalamic osmoreceptors with secondary meningeal vessel dilation. Drinking 500 mL of water provides relief within 30 min in ~47% of dehydration-triggered headaches.

features.evidenceLabel: Complete absence of ipsilateral cranial autonomic features — actively argues against cluster and TAC
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Ipsilateral cranial autonomic features (lacrimation, ptosis, nasal symptoms, conjunctival injection) are a required diagnostic criterion for cluster headache and TACs. Their complete absence is a positive feature for TTH; patients explicitly denying any eye watering, nasal symptoms, or eyelid drooping shift probability strongly away from cluster toward TTH.

features.evidenceLabel: Absence of aura — no visual, sensory, or speech disturbance preceding headache
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Aura (reversible focal neurological symptoms preceding headache) is a required criterion for Migraine With Aura and TIA-related headache. Its absence removes these diagnoses from contention. Explicitly noting that the patient has never experienced visual phenomena, tingling, or speech disturbance before a headache strongly supports TTH over MwA.

features.evidenceLabel: Years-long history of identical headaches with no progression or change in character — reassuring benign pattern
features.citation: Tfelt-Hansen P et al. Headache 2000. A long-standing pattern of identical, non-progressive headaches is the strongest single historical reassurance against secondary headache. New headache in an adult warrants investigation; a 5-year history of identical bilateral pressing headaches that respond to paracetamol and have not progressed clinically supports a benign primary diagnosis.

features.evidenceLabel: Resolution with relaxation, holiday, stress removal, or sleep — confirms psychophysiological mechanism
features.citation: Rasmussen BK. Cephalalgia 1993. TTH headaches characteristically resolve with removal of the precipitating stressor (holiday, weekend, post-deadline), relaxation, and sleep. This responsiveness to psychosocial context is not a feature of migraine (which often persists through rest) and provides useful discriminating history.

features.evidenceLabel: Sustained relief from physiotherapy, cervical mobilisation, or massage — confirms musculoskeletal origin
features.citation: Biondi DM. Curr Pain Headache Rep 2005. Cervicogenic components to TTH respond to physiotherapy, cervical mobilisation, and trigger-point injections. Sustained improvement (not just momentary massage relief) between physiotherapy sessions supports a musculoskeletal mechanism and distinguishes from migraine, which does not respond to cervical treatment.

features.evidenceLabel: Papilloedema on fundoscopy — absolute exclusion for TTH; indicates raised intracranial pressure
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018; Mollan SP et al. Pract Neurol 2018. Papilloedema is an absolute red flag excluding TTH. Raised ICP causes bilateral disc oedema visible on fundoscopy. Causes include idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), space-occupying lesion, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, or hydrocephalus. Immediate neuroimaging and neurology referral are mandatory.

features.evidenceLabel: Headache progressively worsening over days to weeks — red flag for raised ICP or space-occupying lesion
features.citation: NICE CG150 2012; Dodick DW. JAMA 2006. A new or progressively worsening headache pattern over weeks is a red flag criterion mandating imaging. TTH is a stable, non-progressive condition. Progressive intensification suggests increased ICP (tumour, subdural haematoma, IIH), CVST, or infectious meningitis. The SNOOP4 mnemonic: Systemic symptoms, Neurological signs, Onset (sudden), Older age, Papilloedema/positional/progressive.

features.evidenceLabel: Fever accompanying headache — excludes primary TTH; mandates meningitis / encephalitis / systemic infection workup
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018; van de Beek D et al. NEJM 2006. Fever is not a feature of any primary headache disorder; its presence mandates exclusion of infectious causes. In the context of headache, fever should immediately raise bacterial meningitis, viral encephalitis, and cerebral abscess in the differential. Even low-grade fever with a new headache in an immunocompromised patient warrants LP.

features.evidenceLabel: Headache precipitated by coughing, sneezing, Valsalva, or physical exertion — red flag for secondary cause
features.citation: Pascual J et al. Lancet 1996. Cough headache and exertional headache may be primary (benign) but secondary causes (Arnold-Chiari malformation, subarachnoid haemorrhage, cerebral venous thrombosis) must be excluded by neuroimaging. TTH is not triggered by Valsalva or physical exertion; such precipitation should prompt MRI brain and MR angiography.

features.evidenceLabel: Headache maximal on waking / worse in morning — raises concern for raised ICP (IIH, tumour, sleep apnoea)
features.citation: Silberstein SD et al. Neurology 2001. While migraine can wake patients from sleep, headache consistently worst on waking or before arising — especially with nausea — is a pattern associated with raised ICP (idiopathic intracranial hypertension, cerebral oedema, space-occupying lesion) and obstructive sleep apnoea. TTH typically improves with activity and is not characteristically worst at waking.

features.evidenceLabel: Ipsilateral lacrimation, conjunctival injection, ptosis, or nasal symptoms — argues strongly against TTH
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Ipsilateral cranial autonomic features are a required diagnostic criterion for cluster headache and the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TAC). Their presence with a unilateral or bilateral headache essentially excludes TTH as the primary diagnosis and mandates consideration of cluster headache, SUNCT, paroxysmal hemicrania, or a secondary headache with autonomic involvement.
Lipton RB. Headache 2013. Unilateral LR+ 4.0 for migraine
ICHD-3 2018. Pulsating quality — required migraine criterion. LR+ 8.2
ICHD-3. Nausea required criterion. LR+ 5.2 for migraine
ICHD-3. Photophobia required criterion for migraine
Lipton RB. Neurology 2007. Female:male 3:1 for migraine

features.evidenceLabel: Osmophobia — hypersensitivity to smells (highly specific for migraine vs TTH)
features.citation: Kelman L. Cephalalgia 2004. Osmophobia LR+ 5.8 for migraine vs TTH. Present in 43–95% of migraineurs; rare in TTH and SAH. ICHD-3 supplementary criterion.

features.evidenceLabel: Cutaneous allodynia — scalp / skin tenderness during attack
features.citation: Burstein R et al. Ann Neurol 2000. Cutaneous allodynia present in ~70% of migraineurs; peripheral and central sensitisation. Predicts triptan failure if develops before treatment.

features.evidenceLabel: Visual aura — scintillating scotoma / fortification spectra preceding headache
features.citation: Olesen J et al. Lancet Neurol 2004. ICHD-3: visual aura must spread over ≥5 min, last 5–60 min, and fully reverse. Scintillating scotoma pathognomonic for migraine aura.

features.evidenceLabel: Sensory aura — unilateral paraesthesia spreading over 20–30 minutes
features.citation: Russell MB & Olesen J. Brain 1996. Sensory aura (unilateral paraesthesia) present in 31% of migraine with aura; spreading Jacksonian march over 20–30 min distinguishes from TIA (onset seconds).

features.evidenceLabel: Brainstem aura — vertigo, diplopia, tinnitus, dysarthria (vestibular migraine)
features.citation: Lempert T et al. Neurology 2012. Vestibular migraine: recurrent vertigo + migrainous features. ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria. 1% of migraine cases; most common cause of episodic vertigo + headache.

features.evidenceLabel: Prodrome — yawning, food craving, mood change or fatigue hours before headache
features.citation: Giffin NJ et al. Neurology 2003. Prodromal symptoms in 72% of migraineurs; yawning (36%) and food craving (32%) most specific. Reflects hypothalamic activation before trigeminal activation.

features.evidenceLabel: Postdrome — cognitive fog, fatigue, difficulty concentrating after headache resolution
features.citation: Giffin NJ et al. Neurology 2016. Postdrome in 80% of attacks; cognitive impairment, fatigue, neck stiffness. Distinguishes migraine from TTH where attack ends cleanly.

features.evidenceLabel: Family history of migraine in 1st-degree relative
features.citation: Mulder EJ et al. Cephalalgia 2003. Twin studies: heritability 50%. Family history LR+ 3.0 for migraine. CACNA1A / KCNK18 gene variants identified in familial hemiplegic migraine.

features.evidenceLabel: Sleep terminates or relieves attack — characteristic abortive treatment for migraine
features.citation: Blau JN. Lancet 1982. Sleep relieves migraine in >80% when attack allowed to run its natural course. Dark, quiet room + sleep is first-line non-pharmacological treatment.

features.evidenceLabel: Psychological stress or 'let-down' after stress as a precipitant
features.citation: Spierings EL et al. Headache 2001. Stress (emotional / physical) most common trigger in 70–80% of migraineurs. Let-down effect (relaxation after stress) also a recognised trigger.

features.evidenceLabel: Alcohol — especially red wine — as a migraine trigger
features.citation: Panconesi A. J Headache Pain 2008. Alcohol triggers migraine in 30–38%; red wine implicated by sulphites, histamine, tyramine. Occurs within hours, distinguishable from hangover headache.

features.evidenceLabel: Sleep deprivation or oversleeping as a precipitant ('weekend migraine')
features.citation: Kelman L & Rains JC. Headache 2005. Sleep disturbance triggers or worsens migraine in 50%. Both too little and too much sleep are triggers (bidirectional relationship).

features.evidenceLabel: Moderate to severe pain intensity (≥6/10) interfering with daily activities
features.citation: Lipton RB et al. Headache 2001. ICHD-3 criterion: headache must be moderate or severe. Also MIDAS disability ≥11 days/3 months is threshold for preventive therapy.

features.evidenceLabel: Combined oral contraceptive use — hormonal fluctuation as migraine trigger
features.citation: MacGregor EA. Lancet Neurol 2004. Oestrogen withdrawal during pill-free week triggers menstrual migraine. COC contraindicated with migraine with aura (stroke risk Class III/IV WHO-MEC).

features.evidenceLabel: Bilateral pressing / tightening quality — argues for tension-type headache
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Bilateral non-pulsating (pressing/tightening) quality is a positive criterion for TTH and an exclusion criterion for migraine without aura. LR- 0.19 for migraine.

features.evidenceLabel: Thunderclap onset — argues strongly against migraine (raises SAH / RCVS probability)
features.citation: Ducros A & Bousser MG. BMJ 2013. Thunderclap headache is not caused by migraine. Sudden maximal onset mandates exclusion of SAH, RCVS, CVST before diagnosing primary headache disorder.

features.evidenceLabel: Absence of nausea and vomiting — required symptom absent (reduces ICHD-3 probability)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Migraine without aura requires nausea/vomiting OR photophobia+phonophobia. Absence of all three makes diagnosis unlikely.

features.evidenceLabel: Duration <4h — migraine typically lasts 4–72h untreated; shorter attacks suggest cluster or TAC
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. 4–72h duration required for migraine. Attacks <4h suggest cluster headache (15–180 min), SUNCT/SUNA, or indomethacin-responsive headache.

features.evidenceLabel: Failure to respond to two different triptans — reduces migraine probability
features.citation: Scher AI et al. Neurology 2003. Non-response to two triptans has positive predictive value for non-migraine diagnosis; consider secondary headache workup. Also consider medication overuse.

features.evidenceLabel: Compulsion to lie in a dark, quiet room during attack — reflects photo/phonophobia severity
features.citation: Goadsby PJ et al. NEJM 2002. The compulsion to seek a dark, quiet environment is one of the most clinically reliable indicators of migraine severity. It directly reflects the photophobia and phonophobia that are ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria. Unlike TTH patients who can often continue activities, migraineurs are typically disabled and seek refuge from sensory stimulation.

features.evidenceLabel: Consistent relief with NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400–800 mg, naproxen 500–1000 mg, aspirin 900 mg)
features.citation: Tfelt-Hansen P et al. Cephalalgia 2006. NSAIDs are first-line for acute migraine; ibuprofen 400 mg provides relief in ~57%, naproxen 500 mg in ~50% (NNT ~3–5). Regular consistent NSAID response is a positive marker for migraine. Failure of NSAIDs at adequate dose is associated with triptan need and more severe phenotype.

features.evidenceLabel: Response to gepant (ubrogepant, rimegepant) or CGRP monoclonal antibody prevention — near-pathognomonic
features.citation: Dodick DW et al. NEJM 2019 (erenumab); Lipton RB et al. NEJM 2019 (ubrogepant). CGRP pathway drugs (gepants, ditans, anti-CGRP mAbs) are migraine-specific; their therapeutic response is near-pathognomonic for migraine. Response to erenumab, fremanezumab, or galcanezumab preventive therapy with ≥50% headache-day reduction is a definitive positive feature.

features.evidenceLabel: Neck pain as part of migraine attack (trigeminocervical complex activation) — present in up to 75%
features.citation: Bartsch T & Goadsby PJ. Ann Neurol 2003. Neck pain occurs in 38–75% of migraine attacks, reflecting convergence of trigeminal and cervical afferents in the trigeminocervical complex (TCC; C1–C3). Clinically important because neck pain in migraine is often misattributed to 'cervicogenic headache', delaying correct diagnosis. Unlike true cervicogenic headache, migraine neck pain is bilateral, does not restrict cervical ROM, and responds to triptans.

features.evidenceLabel: Excessive yawning as premonitory symptom (hours before headache onset) — most reliable prodromal marker
features.citation: Giffin NJ et al. Neurology 2003. Yawning is the most frequently reported and most reliable premonitory symptom in migraine, present in up to 36% of attacks in prospective diary studies. Patients who recognise yawning as their migraine prodrome can initiate early treatment before pain onset. The mechanism involves dopaminergic hypothalamic activation during the prodrome phase.

features.evidenceLabel: Cognitive impairment during attack ('brain fog') — difficulty concentrating, word-finding, memory
features.citation: Farmer K et al. Curr Pain Headache Rep 2012. Cognitive impairment (brain fog, difficulty concentrating, word-finding problems) affects ~50% of migraineurs during attacks and during the postdrome phase. Its occurrence as a prodromal or ictal symptom is more specific to migraine than TTH, reflecting widespread cortical dysfunction beyond the pain-generating mechanism.

features.evidenceLabel: Bright light, flickering light, or visual stimuli reliably trigger attacks — photosensitivity
features.citation: Mulleners WM et al. Cephalalgia 2001. Photosensitivity (sensitivity to light as a trigger) is reported by 50–60% of migraineurs as a reliable attack precipitant, reflecting cortical hyperexcitability. Fluorescent lighting, sunlight glare, screen flicker, and cinema stroboscopes are the most common light triggers. This is distinct from ictal photophobia (during attack) and reflects interictal cortical susceptibility.

features.evidenceLabel: Weather change or falling barometric pressure as a reliable trigger — reported in 50–75% of migraineurs
features.citation: Scher AI et al. Neurology 2004. Weather-related triggers (barometric pressure drop, storm approach, hot dry winds) are reported by 50–75% of migraineurs. Meteorological triggers are relatively specific to migraine over TTH. The proposed mechanism involves barometric pressure changes directly affecting meningeal nociceptors and modulating thalamic gating of pain signals.

features.evidenceLabel: Tyramine-containing foods (aged cheese, chocolate, red wine, processed meats) as dietary triggers
features.citation: Scharff L et al. Headache 1995. Dietary triggers including tyramine-rich foods (aged cheeses, chocolate, cured meats, red wine) are reported by 20–30% of migraineurs. Chocolate craving in the prodrome phase is often mistaken as the trigger when it is actually the prodrome itself (dopaminergic craving). Dietary triggers are more specific to migraine than TTH.

features.evidenceLabel: Strong odours (perfume, paint, smoke) reliably trigger attacks — olfactory hypersensitivity
features.citation: Kelman L. Cephalalgia 2004. Olfactory triggers are reported by 43% of migraineurs; strong perfume is the most common. This olfactory hypersensitivity reflects interictal central sensitisation and trigeminal nociceptor hyperexcitability. It is a clinically useful trigger history feature that is relatively specific for migraine over TTH.

features.evidenceLabel: Significant headache-related functional disability — unable to work, school absence, bed rest required
features.citation: Lipton RB et al. Headache 2001 (MIDAS). Functional disability distinguishes migraine from TTH at a population level. The MIDAS (Migraine Disability Assessment) questionnaire quantifies lost days; Grade III–IV disability (≥11 lost days/3 months) is almost exclusively due to migraine. TTH rarely causes such severe functional impairment. Disability documentation supports diagnosis and treatment justification.

features.evidenceLabel: Worsening migraine frequency / severity during perimenopause — oestrogen fluctuation mechanism
features.citation: MacGregor EA. Maturitas 2012. Migraine worsens in 45–60% of women during perimenopause due to oestrogen withdrawal and fluctuation; improves after menopause in 67%. Perimenopausal migraine escalation is a recognised clinical pattern. Conversely, migraine improvement in early pregnancy (oestrogen rise) and worsening postpartum (oestrogen drop) are also characteristic hormonal signatures.

features.evidenceLabel: Papilloedema — absolute exclusion for primary migraine; indicates raised intracranial pressure
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Papilloedema on fundoscopy excludes all primary headache disorders. It indicates raised ICP from space-occupying lesion, IIH, cerebral venous thrombosis, or hydrocephalus. A patient presenting with 'migraine-like' headache and papilloedema has a secondary headache until proven otherwise. Urgent neuroimaging is mandatory before any lumbar puncture attempt.

features.evidenceLabel: Neck stiffness / nuchal rigidity — excludes primary migraine; mandates meningitis / SAH exclusion
features.citation: van de Beek D et al. NEJM 2006; ICHD-3 2018. Meningism (neck stiffness, Kernig's/Brudzinski's signs) is not a feature of migraine and mandates urgent exclusion of bacterial meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, and viral encephalitis. Neck pain in migraine is a subjective symptom without true meningism; objective nuchal rigidity on examination is a red flag requiring LP after neuroimaging.

features.evidenceLabel: Fever accompanying headache — excludes primary migraine; infection workup mandatory
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Fever is not a feature of migraine. Its presence with headache mandates exclusion of bacterial meningitis, viral encephalitis, cerebral abscess, systemic viral illness with headache, and SARS-CoV-2. Even a fever of 37.8°C with a new or changed headache in a patient with a prior migraine history warrants reassessment for secondary cause.

features.evidenceLabel: Absence of BOTH photophobia and phonophobia — fails ICHD-3 C criterion for migraine
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Migraine Without Aura requires at least one of: nausea/vomiting, OR photophobia AND phonophobia (criterion C). If the patient explicitly denies both photophobia and phonophobia, the ICHD-3 C criterion can only be met by nausea/vomiting alone. Complete absence of photophobia, phonophobia, and nausea eliminates migraine and strongly supports TTH or secondary headache.

features.evidenceLabel: Persistent focal neurological deficit — not explained by typical migraine aura; secondary cause
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018; Silberstein SD. Lancet Neurol 2004. Migraine aura produces fully reversible neurological symptoms lasting 5–60 min. Persistent (>60 min) or progressive neurological deficits in the context of headache mandate urgent secondary workup: ischaemic stroke, cerebral venous thrombosis, CADASIL, and mitochondrial disorders all present with headache plus deficits. Hemiplegic migraine is a rare exception but requires specialist confirmation.
ICHD-3 2018. Strictly unilateral is required criterion for cluster headache
ICHD-3. Severe / very severe required criterion
ICHD-3. Autonomic features LR+ >10 for cluster

features.evidenceLabel: Restlessness / agitation (cannot lie still — opposite to migraine)

features.citation: Headache Classification Committee ICHD-3. Male predominance 4–8:1

features.evidenceLabel: Orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain — ICHD-3 required location
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Cluster headache pain is centred on the orbit, supraorbital region, or temporal area in virtually all cases; strictly ipsilateral. Orbital 'boring' or 'stabbing' quality is most characteristic.

features.evidenceLabel: Boring / stabbing / searing quality — distinct from the pressing TTH or pulsating migraine
features.citation: Headache Classification Committee. Cephalalgia 2018. Cluster headache quality described as 'boring', 'stabbing', 'red-hot poker through the eye'. Sharp stabbing quality distinguishes from other primary headaches.

features.evidenceLabel: Ipsilateral conjunctival injection / eye redness — cranial autonomic feature
features.citation: May A et al. Brain 1998. Conjunctival injection present in 79% of cluster attacks; reflects trigeminal-autonomic arc activation. Ipsilateral parasympathetic activation via sphenopalatine ganglion.

features.evidenceLabel: Ipsilateral nasal congestion or rhinorrhoea during attack
features.citation: Goadsby PJ et al. Lancet 2001. Nasal autonomic features (rhinorrhoea 36%, congestion 48%) are ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms present in most cluster attacks; reflect parasympathetic sphenopalatine activation.

features.evidenceLabel: Ipsilateral forehead and facial sweating / flushing during attack
features.citation: Ekbom K & Lindgren L. Headache 1971. Facial sweating and flushing present in ~50% of cluster attacks; ipsilateral autonomic activation pattern. Part of ICHD-3 diagnostic criterion for cranial autonomic features.

features.evidenceLabel: Strict circadian pattern — attacks at same time each day (often 1–2 AM)
features.citation: Kudrow L. Headache 1987. Attacks occur in clusters of weeks-months, with remarkable circadian regularity (same time ± 30 min each day). Hypothalamic circadian pacemaker involvement confirmed by PET. Pathognomonic temporal pattern.

features.evidenceLabel: Annual or seasonal periodicity — bouts at the same time each year
features.citation: Waldenlind E et al. Cephalalgia 1987. Seasonal clustering in ~50% of episodic cluster headache; spring and autumn equinox most common. Implies circannual chronobiological mechanism linked to photoperiod.

features.evidenceLabel: Episodic cluster period 6–12 weeks followed by remission of months to years
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Episodic cluster headache (85% of cases): bouts lasting 6–12 weeks, separated by remissions ≥3 months. Chronic cluster (15%): attacks for >1 year without ≥3-month remission.

features.evidenceLabel: Alcohol reliably triggers attack during a cluster bout (not outside a bout)
features.citation: Ekbom K. Headache 1974. Small amounts of alcohol (1–2 units) trigger cluster attack within 30–60 min in >50% during an active bout; the same patient is immune to alcohol between bouts. This on-off pattern is pathognomonic.

features.evidenceLabel: Glyceryl trinitrate / nitroglycerin reliably provokes attack during active bout
features.citation: Tassorelli C et al. Cephalalgia 2005. GTN triggers cluster attacks within 30–45 min in patients during active bout; used diagnostically and in research. Also: histamine, hypoxia trigger attacks during a bout.

features.evidenceLabel: Rapid relief with 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask (12–15 L/min for 15 min)
features.citation: Cohen AS et al. JAMA 2009. High-flow O2 aborts cluster attack in 78% vs 20% placebo (NNT 1.7). EAN/EFNS Class A recommendation. Mechanism: reversal of vasodilation via vasoconstriction of trigeminovascular complex.

features.evidenceLabel: Subcutaneous sumatriptan 6mg — aborts attack within 15 minutes
features.citation: Ekbom K et al. Cephalalgia 1993. SC sumatriptan relief at 15 min: 74% vs 26% placebo (NNT 2.1). Most effective acute treatment. Intranasal zolmitriptan 5–10mg an alternative when injection declined.

features.evidenceLabel: Partial Horner's syndrome — persistent ptosis / miosis between attacks
features.citation: Salvesen R. Headache 2006. Persistent partial Horner's syndrome (ptosis + miosis) between attacks in 4–5% of cluster patients; indicates damage to pericarotid sympathetic fibres from repeated pericarotid inflammation.

features.evidenceLabel: Male, age 20–50 — peak demographic (M:F ratio 5:1, mean onset age 30)
features.citation: Torelli P & Manzoni GC. J Headache Pain 2003. Male predominance 5:1; peak onset 20–40y. Unlike migraine, no hormonal association. Lean body habitus (leonine facies) classically described.

features.evidenceLabel: Family history of cluster headache (14× increased risk in first-degree relatives)
features.citation: Leone M et al. Neurology 2001. First-degree relatives have 14× increased risk vs general population; 2–7% familial cases. Autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance proposed.

features.evidenceLabel: Bilateral pain — strictly excludes cluster headache (must be unilateral)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Cluster headache must be strictly unilateral; bilateral onset is an absolute exclusion criterion. Bilateral severe headache with autonomic features suggests SUNCT/SUNA or secondary cause.

features.evidenceLabel: Pressing / tightening quality — argues against cluster (which is boring/stabbing)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Cluster headache quality is boring or stabbing, never pressing or tightening (which characterises TTH). Quality mismatch substantially reduces cluster probability.

features.evidenceLabel: Absent ipsilateral autonomic features — required for cluster headache diagnosis
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. At least one ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptom (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal symptoms, ptosis, miosis, forehead sweating, ear fullness) is a required criterion for cluster headache.

features.evidenceLabel: Patient lies still during attack — argues against cluster (which causes agitation)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Restlessness or agitation is a characteristic feature of cluster headache (patient paces, rocks). Lying still is characteristic of migraine. Behaviour during attack is a key discriminating feature.

features.evidenceLabel: Duration >3 hours — cluster headache lasts 15–180 min; longer attacks suggest migraine
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Upper duration limit for cluster headache is 180 minutes. Attacks consistently lasting >3h are more consistent with migraine without aura. Consider TAC overlap syndromes.

features.evidenceLabel: Duration <15 minutes — too brief for cluster; consider SUNCT (1–600 sec) or SUNA
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Minimum cluster headache duration is 15 minutes. Attacks <15 min with autonomic features suggest SUNCT (Short-lasting Unilateral Neuralgiform headache with Conjunctival injection and Tearing).

features.evidenceLabel: Ipsilateral eyelid oedema / periorbital swelling — ICHD-3 cranial autonomic criterion
features.citation: Headache Classification Committee. Cephalalgia 2018. Ipsilateral eyelid oedema is one of 7 listed ICHD-3 cranial autonomic symptoms (criterion B). Present in ~40% of attacks; reflects pericarotid parasympathetic activation via the sphenopalatine ganglion.

features.evidenceLabel: Ipsilateral ear fullness / aural pressure — ICHD-3 cranial autonomic criterion
features.citation: Headache Classification Committee. Cephalalgia 2018. Aural fullness is listed as one of 7 ICHD-3 cranial autonomic features for cluster headache. Present in ~25% of attacks; often combined with nasal congestion. Reflects shared sphenopalatine ganglion innervation of the eustachian tube.

features.evidenceLabel: Multiple attacks per day (1–8 per 24h) — pathognomonic frequency for cluster
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018; Torelli P & Manzoni GC. J Headache Pain 2003. Cluster headache occurs in bouts of 1–8 attacks per 24 hours; this high daily frequency is pathognomonic and sharply distinguishes it from migraine (1–2/month) and TTH. Mean 1.5 attacks/day; frequency peaks mid-bout.

features.evidenceLabel: Woken from REM sleep 60–90 min after sleep onset — classic nocturnal cluster pattern
features.citation: Kudrow L. Headache 1987; Pfaffenrath V et al. Cephalalgia 1986. 60–75% of cluster attacks wake the patient from sleep, characteristically 60–90 min after sleep onset (first REM period). This REM-linked onset is a reliable clinical marker; PET studies confirm hypothalamic activation coinciding with circadian and REM rhythms.

features.evidenceLabel: Rapid escalation to maximum intensity within 5–15 minutes — unlike the 1–2h build of migraine
features.citation: Ekbom K. Cephalalgia 1990. Cluster headache escalates to peak intensity within 5–15 minutes; the explosive ramp-up contrasts with migraine's gradual 1–2 hour build and is a clinically useful differentiating feature when taking a history of attack evolution.

features.evidenceLabel: Prophylactic response to verapamil (240–960 mg/day) — first-line EAN/EFNS preventive
features.citation: Leone M et al. Neurology 2000; EAN/EFNS 2016 guidelines. Verapamil is the first-line preventive for cluster headache (Class A evidence). Response to verapamil at doses of 240–960 mg/day (higher than cardiac doses) is near-pathognomonic for cluster; migraine, TTH, and SUNCT typically do not respond to verapamil at these doses.

features.evidenceLabel: Rapid suppression with oral prednisolone bridging course (60–100 mg/day tapering) during active bout
features.citation: Tfelt-Hansen PC et al. Cephalalgia 1983; EAN/EFNS 2016. Oral prednisolone or IM/IV methylprednisolone provides rapid transitional suppression of cluster bouts within 2–5 days in most patients. This brisk corticosteroid response, combined with the circadian bout pattern, is clinically distinctive for cluster headache.

features.evidenceLabel: History of previous episodic cluster bouts with full remissions — strongest historical predictor
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018; Torelli P & Manzoni GC. J Headache Pain 2003. A history of identical episodic bouts lasting 6–12 weeks separated by complete pain-free remissions ≥3 months is the most specific historical feature for episodic cluster headache. Patients often describe the same annual pattern for decades.

features.evidenceLabel: Chronic cluster headache — attacks for >1 year without ≥3-month remission (15% of cluster patients)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Chronic cluster headache affects ~15% of patients; attacks occur daily or near-daily for >1 year without a remission period ≥3 months. Recognition is important as treatment (verapamil, lithium) differs from episodic management and long-term neurological review is required.

features.evidenceLabel: Suicidal ideation or self-harm urge during attack ('suicide headache') — reflects extreme severity
features.citation: Rozen TD & Fishman RS. Headache 2012. Cluster headache is nicknamed 'suicide headache'; 55% of patients in surveys reported suicidal ideation during attacks. While not an ICHD-3 criterion, its presence in the context of severe orbital attacks is a strong positive predictor, and its recognition is clinically vital for patient safety.

features.evidenceLabel: Hot bath / shower or heat triggers attack during active bout — vasodilator mechanism
features.citation: Kudrow L. Headache 1974. Vasodilatory stimuli including hot baths, saunas, and fever trigger cluster attacks during an active bout in ~30% of patients. The same patient is immune to identical stimuli during remission — the on/off nature of this susceptibility is pathognomonic for cluster, paralleling the alcohol trigger pattern.

features.evidenceLabel: High altitude / air travel triggers attacks — hypoxia-mediated vasodilation during active bout
features.citation: Millson DS et al. Headache 1996. Hypoxia from altitude (>2500 m) or cabin pressure in aircraft triggers cluster attacks during a bout in susceptible patients. Oxygen supplementation both prevents and aborts these altitude-induced attacks, consistent with the proven mechanism of high-flow O2 in acute treatment.

features.evidenceLabel: Non-pulsating / non-throbbing quality — cluster is boring/stabbing, never pulsating like migraine
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018; Sjostrand C et al. Cephalalgia 2010. Cluster headache pain is boring, stabbing, or burning — never pulsating or throbbing. Pulsating quality is a positive criterion for migraine. Non-pulsating character is a useful negative discriminator: it argues against migraine while supporting cluster, TTH, or a secondary headache.

features.evidenceLabel: Premonitory / prodromal symptoms (mood, yawning, food craving) — argues strongly for migraine not cluster
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018; Giffin NJ et al. Neurology 2003. Premonitory symptoms (fatigue, yawning, food craving, mood change) occur in 60–80% of migraines and are a recognised ICHD-3 feature. Cluster headache characteristically lacks a premonitory phase — onset is abrupt without warning, which is part of its alarming quality. Their presence substantially favours migraine.

features.evidenceLabel: Duration in seconds to a few minutes — too brief for cluster; strongly suggests SUNCT or SUNA
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. SUNCT (Short-lasting Unilateral Neuralgiform headache with Conjunctival injection and Tearing) lasts 1–600 seconds; SUNA lasts 1 second to 10 minutes. Both mimic cluster with ipsilateral autonomic features but occur at much higher frequency (up to 200/day) and have much shorter duration. Attacks lasting only seconds exclude cluster headache.

features.evidenceLabel: Prominent nausea and vomiting as chief associated symptom — characteristic of migraine, not cluster
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. While mild nausea can occur in cluster headache, prominent nausea and vomiting as the dominant associated feature is characteristic of migraine (one of two required associated criteria). In cluster headache, autonomic features (lacrimation, nasal symptoms, ptosis) dominate. Prominent GI symptoms shift probability toward migraine.

features.evidenceLabel: Thunderclap onset — 'worst headache of life' — RED FLAG
features.citation: Perry JJ et al. BMJ 2011. Thunderclap headache sensitivity 98.5% for SAH. 'Worst ever' headache LR+ 11.0

features.evidenceLabel: Sudden onset at maximal severity within seconds

features.citation: Edlow JA et al. Ann Emerg Med 2000. Neck stiffness LR+ 6.6 for SAH
Perry JJ. Lancet 2011. CT sensitivity 98% within 6h of onset

features.evidenceLabel: Sentinel / warning headache days before — prodromal minor bleed
features.citation: Backes D et al. Stroke 2012. Sentinel headache precedes 20–40% of SAH. LR+ ~7.0. Prompt re-presentation avoids delayed diagnosis.

features.evidenceLabel: Onset during exertion / straining / sexual activity (Valsalva)
features.citation: Feigin VL et al. Lancet Neurol 2009. Strenuous physical activity and sexual activity are established precipitants of aneurysmal rupture. OR 3.5–10.

features.evidenceLabel: Occipital / nuchal pain radiating to neck and back
features.citation: Linn FH et al. Lancet 1994. Occipital onset with radiation to neck and back is characteristic of SAH; blood tracks posteriorly and down the spinal canal.

features.evidenceLabel: 'Worst headache of life' — maximal severity at onset (10/10)
features.citation: Perry JJ et al. CMAJ 2010. Severity 'worst ever' LR+ 11.0 for SAH vs other thunderclap headaches.

features.evidenceLabel: Kernig's / Brudzinski's sign — meningeal irritation by subarachnoid blood
features.citation: Thomas KE et al. Lancet 2002. Kernig's LR+ 6.1, Brudzinski's LR+ 4.3 for bacterial meningitis; also positive in SAH as blood causes chemical meningism.

features.evidenceLabel: Ipsilateral CN III palsy — posterior communicating artery aneurysm
features.citation: Kissel JT et al. JAMA 1983. Isolated pupil-involving CN III palsy: aneurysm (PCoA) sensitivity 97%, specificity 99%. Treat as aneurysm until proven otherwise.

features.evidenceLabel: Unilateral fixed dilated pupil — CN III compression / transtentorial herniation
features.citation: Connolly ES et al. Stroke 2012. Fixed dilated pupil in SAH indicates imminent herniation — neurosurgical emergency. AHA/ASA Class I recommendation for immediate imaging.

features.evidenceLabel: Retinal / preretinal haemorrhage — Terson syndrome (vitreous bleed)
features.citation: Pfausler B et al. J Neurosurg 1996. Terson syndrome (vitreous / preretinal haemorrhage) present in 13% of SAH; associated with higher Hunt-Hess grade. Specificity near 100% for SAH when present.

features.evidenceLabel: Focal neurological deficit — hemiparesis, dysphasia, or cranial nerve palsy
features.citation: van Gijn J et al. Lancet 2007. Focal deficits in SAH indicate parenchymal involvement, vasospasm, or intracerebral haematoma from aneurysm rupture.

features.evidenceLabel: Back pain / leg pain — subarachnoid blood tracking down the spinal canal
features.citation: Linn FH et al. Lancet 1994. Lumbar back pain and bilateral leg pain from lumbar nerve root irritation occurs as blood descends the subarachnoid space.

features.evidenceLabel: Family history of SAH or intracranial aneurysm in 1st-degree relative
features.citation: Broderick JP et al. Stroke 2009. First-degree relative with SAH: RR 3–7. Familial SAH accounts for 5–20% of cases. Indicates heritable aneurysm susceptibility.

features.evidenceLabel: Polycystic kidney disease — 10× increased risk of intracranial aneurysm
features.citation: Chapman AB et al. J Am Soc Nephrol 1992. Prevalence of intracranial aneurysm in ADPKD: 8% (vs 1–2% general population). PKD1 gene mutation particularly associated.

features.evidenceLabel: Hypertension — established risk factor for aneurysm formation and rupture
features.citation: Feigin VL et al. Lancet Neurol 2009. Hypertension OR 2.5 for SAH; accounts for ~25% of attributable risk. Systolic >160 associated with 4× rupture rate.

features.evidenceLabel: Smoking — doubles SAH risk; dose-dependent relationship
features.citation: Broderick JP et al. Stroke 1994. Smoking RR 2.2 for SAH; pack-years correlated with risk. Current smokers have higher aneurysm rupture rates than ex-smokers.

features.evidenceLabel: Age 40–65 — peak incidence of aneurysmal SAH (mean age 55)
features.citation: de Rooij NK et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2007. Incidence peaks 55–65y. SAH accounts for 5% of all strokes but 27% of stroke-related life-years lost.

features.evidenceLabel: CT angiography — cerebral aneurysm identified (site, size, morphology)
features.citation: van der Schaaf I et al. Stroke 2005. CT angiography sensitivity 97.7% for aneurysms ≥4mm; replaces catheter angiography as first-line in acute SAH workup.

features.evidenceLabel: MRI FLAIR — subarachnoid hyperintensity (more sensitive than CT after 24h)
features.citation: Verma RK et al. Radiology 2013. FLAIR MRI sensitivity 87–100% for SAH >24h old (CT sensitivity drops to 50% at 5–7 days). Essential for late-presenting cases.

features.evidenceLabel: Gradual onset over hours — argues strongly against SAH (which is instantaneous)
features.citation: Perry JJ et al. BMJ 2011. Ottawa SAH Rule excludes thunderclap headaches reaching peak in >1h. Gradual-onset headache LR- 0.08 for SAH.

features.evidenceLabel: Previous identical headaches — establishes recurrent benign headache pattern
features.citation: Linn FHH et al. Neurology 1998. In thunderclap headache, a prior identical episode reduces SAH probability; Ottawa Rule includes this as exclusion criterion.

features.evidenceLabel: Mild intensity (≤5/10) — SAH is typically the worst pain ever experienced
features.citation: Perry JJ et al. CMAJ 2010. Severity ≤5/10 significantly reduces SAH likelihood. Most SAH patients rate pain 8–10/10.

features.evidenceLabel: Seizure at onset of thunderclap headache — aneurysmal rupture with cortical spreading
features.citation: Butzkueven H et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2000. Seizure occurs at ictus in 6–16% of aneurysmal SAH and in up to 26% of anterior communicating artery aneurysms. Onset seizure with thunderclap headache is a highly specific combination for SAH. Late seizures (>24h post-ictus) reflect cortical irritation from subarachnoid blood and are an independent risk factor for delayed cerebral ischaemia.

features.evidenceLabel: Diplopia at headache onset — CN III or CN VI palsy from aneurysmal compression or raised ICP
features.citation: Giombini S et al. J Neurosurg 1984. Diplopia at SAH onset reflects CN III palsy (posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing the nerve from outside — pupil-involving, downward and outward gaze deviation), CN VI palsy (false localising from raised ICP), or cavernous sinus involvement. Painful diplopia with headache is a neurosurgical emergency.

features.evidenceLabel: Thunderclap headache waking patient from sleep — SAH until proven otherwise
features.citation: Perry JJ et al. BMJ 2011 (Ottawa SAH Rule). Being woken from sleep by a thunderclap headache is a high-risk feature; SAH must be excluded. Thunderclap onset during sleep is less amenable to a gradual-onset alternative explanation, making benign causes less plausible. Combined with maximal severity at onset and no prior history of identical headaches, this warrants emergency CT.

features.evidenceLabel: Reactive fever 6–24h after thunderclap headache onset — meningeal irritation from subarachnoid blood
features.citation: Rabinstein AA et al. Neurocrit Care 2004. Fever developing 6–24 hours after SAH onset reflects chemical meningitis from subarachnoid blood products; it is not a primary infectious process. Fever is present in up to 72% of SAH during the hospital course. Early fever (within 24h) correlates with haemorrhage volume and predicts delayed cerebral ischaemia; it is distinct from the fever of bacterial meningitis which precedes or accompanies the headache.

features.evidenceLabel: Neurological deterioration 4–14 days post-ictus — vasospasm / delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI)
features.citation: Vergouwen MD et al. Stroke 2010. Delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) complicates 20–30% of aneurysmal SAH, typically presenting 4–14 days post-ictus with new focal deficit, confusion, or declining GCS. It reflects cerebral vasospasm plus microthrombosis and cortical spreading depolarisations. Nimodipine reduces DCI (NNT ~15). Deterioration in this time window after a confirmed SAH is DCI until proven otherwise.

features.evidenceLabel: Acute obstructive hydrocephalus — blood in ventricles/CSF pathways; rapid GCS decline within hours
features.citation: van Gijn J et al. Lancet 2007. Acute hydrocephalus complicates 20–30% of aneurysmal SAH; it results from obstruction of CSF pathways by subarachnoid/intraventricular blood. Clinical presentation: rapid decline in GCS, upgaze palsy, small unreactive pupils. Emergency ventriculostomy is life-saving. Early hydrocephalus on CT predicts worse functional outcome and rebleeding risk.

features.evidenceLabel: GCS ≤14 at presentation — WFNS grade II–V; predicts outcome and rebleeding risk
features.citation: Drake CG. J Neurosurg 1988 (WFNS scale). GCS at presentation is the basis of the WFNS (World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies) grading scale: Grade I (GCS 15, no deficit), Grade II (GCS 13–14, no deficit), Grade III (GCS 13–14 + focal deficit), Grades IV–V (GCS ≤12). WFNS grade III–V carries 30-day mortality >50%. GCS ≤14 with thunderclap headache is a neurosurgical emergency.

features.evidenceLabel: Digital subtraction angiography — gold standard for aneurysm characterisation; defines neck and morphology
features.citation: van Gijn J et al. Lancet 2007. DSA is the gold standard for cerebral aneurysm detection and characterisation (sensitivity ~95–99% for aneurysms >3 mm). It defines the aneurysm neck, size, orientation, and relationship to parent vessels — essential for surgical clipping or endovascular coiling decisions. CTA is first-line in acute SAH; DSA follows when CTA is equivocal or negative despite confirmed SAH.

features.evidenceLabel: ECG: T-wave inversion, QTc prolongation, ST changes, U-waves — neurogenic cardiac injury from catecholamine surge
features.citation: Sommargren CE. J Neurosci Nurs 2002; Di Pasquale G et al. Stroke 1987. ECG abnormalities occur in 50–80% of SAH; they reflect massive catecholamine release at rupture causing neurogenic myocardial injury (takotsubo-like). Characteristic patterns: diffuse T-wave inversion, QTc prolongation (>500ms — VF risk), ST elevation/depression, prominent U-waves. ECG should be obtained in all suspected SAH; abnormalities do not require cardiac-focused management unless haemodynamically unstable.

features.evidenceLabel: Elevated troponin — neurogenic myocardial injury (not primary ACS) in 20–30% of SAH
features.citation: Tung P et al. Neurocrit Care 2004. Troponin elevation occurs in 20–30% of SAH from neurogenic myocardial injury (catecholamine-mediated subendocardial ischaemia). It is not primary ACS; coronary angiography is not required unless regional wall motion abnormality is severe. Troponin elevation in SAH independently predicts delayed cerebral ischaemia and poor outcome. Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy occurs in ~2% of SAH.

features.evidenceLabel: Prior SAH or known untreated / partially treated aneurysm — extremely high rerupture risk
features.citation: Juvela S et al. Stroke 2000. Untreated aneurysms have an annual rupture risk of 1–2% (ISUIA); prior SAH from a different aneurysm or an incompletely treated aneurysm carries substantially higher risk. A patient presenting with thunderclap headache and a known aneurysm has SAH until proven otherwise, regardless of CT result, and requires DSA.

features.evidenceLabel: Recent cocaine, amphetamine, or sympathomimetic use — abrupt BP surge triggers aneurysm rupture
features.citation: Nanda A et al. J Stroke Cerebrovasc Dis 2000. Cocaine and amphetamines cause abrupt hypertensive surges that can rupture pre-existing intracranial aneurysms. Cocaine-associated SAH is the most common non-traumatic cause of intracranial haemorrhage in adults under 45. Onset is typically within 3 hours of use. Toxicology screen should be included in the SAH workup in young patients.

features.evidenceLabel: Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos Type IV (vascular), or neurofibromatosis — aneurysm association
features.citation: Schievink WI. NEJM 1997. Vascular connective tissue disorders (Ehlers-Danlos Type IV, Marfan syndrome, pseudoxanthoma elasticum) are associated with intracranial aneurysm formation due to abnormal vessel wall collagen. Ehlers-Danlos Type IV carries the highest risk (COL3A1 mutation). When a young patient presents with SAH and features of CTD (aortic root, lens dislocation, skin hyperextensibility), CTD workup is warranted.

features.evidenceLabel: Female sex, particularly post-menopause — 1.6:1 F:M ratio in aneurysmal SAH; oestrogen-protective effect lost
features.citation: Longstreth WT et al. Neurology 1993. SAH is 1.6× more common in women than men overall; the female predominance becomes more pronounced after menopause, suggesting a protective role of oestrogen on aneurysm wall integrity. Female sex combined with hypertension and smoking gives the highest risk. Female sex alone provides a modest positive LR for SAH over primary headache.

features.value: CT negative within 6h AND LP normal
features.evidenceLabel: CT negative within 6h of onset AND normal LP — Ottawa rule negative; effectively excludes SAH
features.citation: Perry JJ et al. NEJM 2011 (Ottawa SAH Rule). Third/fourth-generation CT within 6h of onset has 98.7% sensitivity (100% in prospective validation). When CT within 6h is negative, LP adds sensitivity for xanthochromia (spectrophotometry) for the remaining 1.3%. CT negative <6h + LP normal (no xanthochromia, no RBC) has a negative predictive value of >99.9% for aneurysmal SAH in alert patients. This combination permits safe discharge from emergency.

features.evidenceLabel: Positional headache — worse upright, relieved lying down — suggests intracranial hypotension (CSF leak)
features.citation: Schievink WI. NEJM 2006. Orthostatic headache (worse within 15 min of standing, relieved within 30 min of lying down) is the hallmark of intracranial hypotension from spontaneous CSF leak. It is distinct from SAH headache, which is constant and worsened by any movement or light. A clear orthostatic component substantially reduces SAH probability and suggests spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) or post-LP headache.
van de Beek D. NEJM 2004. Classical triad present in 44%; any two of three in 95%
van de Beek D. NEJM 2004. Neck stiffness LR+ 9.6 (6.1–15.4)
Thompson MJ et al. Lancet 2006. Non-blanching rash LR+ 19.1

features.evidenceLabel: LP — turbid CSF, raised WCC, low glucose
Jolt accentuation — headache worsens on rapid horizontal head rotation (2–3 Hz)
features.citation: Uchihara T & Tsukagoshi H. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1991. Sensitivity 97%, specificity 60% for meningeal irritation. LR+ 11.0. Useful bedside test when formal Kernig/Brudzinski equivocal.

features.evidenceLabel: Papilloedema — raised intracranial pressure; warrants CT before LP
features.citation: van de Beek D et al. NEJM 2004. Papilloedema in 8% of bacterial meningitis. IDSA guidelines: CT before LP if papilloedema, focal deficit, new-onset seizure, immunocompromised, or altered consciousness.

features.evidenceLabel: Non-blanching petechial rash — glass test positive (meningococcaemia)
features.citation: Wells LC et al. Arch Dis Child 2001. Non-blanching rash sensitivity 72%, specificity 96% for meningococcal disease. ANY non-blanching rash = immediate parenteral benzylpenicillin before transfer.

features.evidenceLabel: Seizure at onset or during illness — occurs in ~30% of bacterial meningitis
features.citation: van de Beek D et al. NEJM 2004. New-onset seizure present in 5–28% at onset; associated with higher mortality. Indicates cortical irritation / cerebral oedema / cortical venous thrombosis.

features.evidenceLabel: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome — bilateral adrenal haemorrhage / purpura fulminans / shock
features.citation: Quagliarello VJ & Scheld WM. NEJM 1997. Fulminant meningococcaemia with bilateral adrenal haemorrhage. Purpura fulminans, haemodynamic collapse; mortality >50% without immediate management.

features.evidenceLabel: Sensorineural hearing loss — cochlear damage from inflammatory mediators
features.citation: Dodge PR et al. NEJM 1984. SNHL in 10–30% of survivors; most common neurological sequela. Due to cochlear labyrinthitis from subarachnoid space inflammation. Dexamethasone reduces risk (de Gans NEJM 2002).

features.evidenceLabel: Preceding upper respiratory tract infection — source of haematogenous spread
features.citation: Stephens DS et al. Lancet 2007. Nasopharyngeal colonisation with N. meningitidis precedes haematogenous spread. Preceding viral URTI disrupts mucosal barriers and facilitates invasion.

features.evidenceLabel: Immunocompromised / asplenic / complement deficiency — high-risk host
features.citation: van de Beek D et al. Clin Infect Dis 2006. Asplenia, complement deficiency (C5-C9), and HIV are major risk factors for encapsulated organism meningitis (Neisseria, Pneumococcus, Haemophilus).

features.evidenceLabel: Close contact with confirmed case / freshers / military barracks / Hajj travel
features.citation: Caugant DA & Maiden MC. Vaccine 2009. Clustering in closed communities (university, military) reflects shared carriage. Secondary attack rate 500–1200× general population; prophylaxis required for close contacts.

features.evidenceLabel: Travel to sub-Saharan African meningitis belt (Niger, Mali, Chad region)
features.citation: Greenwood B. Vaccine 1999. The meningitis belt (10°–15°N) has incidence 10–25/100,000; epidemic serogroup A/W135 disease. MenACWY vaccination required for Hajj by Saudi MOH.

features.evidenceLabel: CSF glucose <2.2 mmol/L or CSF:serum ratio <0.4 — hallmark of bacterial meningitis
features.citation: Spanos A et al. JAMA 1989. CSF glucose <2.2 mmol/L LR+ 18.3; CSF:serum ratio <0.4 LR+ 14.7. Glucose consumed by bacteria and neutrophils. Check paired serum glucose at LP.

features.evidenceLabel: CSF protein >1 g/L — elevated protein from blood-brain barrier breakdown
features.citation: Spanos A et al. JAMA 1989. CSF protein >1g/L LR+ 11.1 for bacterial vs viral meningitis. Protein >3g/L associated with poor prognosis (obliterative vasculitis).

features.evidenceLabel: CSF lactate >3.5 mmol/L — anaerobic metabolism by bacteria / ischaemic neurons
features.citation: Sakushima K et al. J Infect 2011. CSF lactate LR+ 21.3 for bacterial vs viral meningitis (sensitivity 93%, specificity 96%). Particularly useful post-antibiotics when cultures may be negative.

features.evidenceLabel: CSF Gram stain positive — organisms visualised (Gram-negative diplococci, Gram-positive cocci)
features.citation: Tunkel AR et al. Clin Infect Dis 2004. Gram stain sensitivity 60–90% (highest for pneumococcal); specificity ~100%. Identifies organism in 80% of untreated cases. Start empirical treatment before result.

features.evidenceLabel: Meningococcal / pneumococcal PCR or antigen detection positive
features.citation: Thulin Hedberg S et al. FEMS Microbiol Rev 2022. PCR sensitivity 95% vs culture 80%; remains positive after antibiotics. N. meningitidis PCR (ctrA gene) recommended for all suspected cases.

features.evidenceLabel: Procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL — elevated in bacterial, normal in viral meningitis
features.citation: Vikse J et al. Infect Dis 2015. Serum procalcitonin LR+ 8.0, LR- 0.08 for bacterial vs viral/aseptic meningitis. Distinguishes bacterial from viral in emergency settings before CSF results available.

features.evidenceLabel: Afebrile at presentation — absence of fever argues strongly against bacterial meningitis
features.citation: van de Beek D et al. NEJM 2004. Fever present in 95% of adult bacterial meningitis. Afebrile presentation unusual (immunosuppressed, elderly on NSAIDs); absence should prompt alternative diagnosis.

features.evidenceLabel: Fully vaccinated against Hib, MenACWY, and PCV — significantly reduces probability
features.citation: Meningitis Research Foundation 2020. MenC vaccination reduced incidence 99% in UK. PCV13 reduced pneumococcal meningitis 64%. Vaccination history is the most important negative risk factor.

features.evidenceLabel: Subacute onset over days — suggests TB meningitis, viral, or fungal rather than bacterial
features.citation: Thwaites GE et al. NEJM 2004. TB meningitis onset 14–40 days; bacterial meningitis typically <24h. Subacute course with prodromal illness favours TB meningitis or viral / cryptococcal aetiology.

features.evidenceLabel: CSF clear, normal glucose, normal protein, no pleocytosis — excludes bacterial meningitis
features.citation: Tunkel AR et al. Clin Infect Dis 2004. Normal CSF (clear, glucose >2.5, protein <0.45g/L, WCC <5) has LR- 0.03 for bacterial meningitis. Rare exception: very early bacterial meningitis before pleocytosis develops.

features.evidenceLabel: Severe, constant, diffuse headache — cardinal symptom; worsened by movement and light
features.citation: van de Beek D et al. NEJM 2006. Headache is present in 87% of adult bacterial meningitis; typically described as the worst headache of the patient's life, diffuse, constant, and worsened by head movement, light, and sound. The combination of severe headache, fever, and neck stiffness is present in only 44% at presentation but its absence does not exclude the diagnosis.

features.evidenceLabel: Vomiting accompanying fever and headache — present in ~30% of bacterial meningitis at presentation
features.citation: van de Beek D et al. NEJM 2006. Vomiting occurs in approximately 30% of adult bacterial meningitis cases. In children and adolescents the proportion is higher (~50%). Nausea and vomiting reflect meningeal irritation and raised ICP. The triad of vomiting, fever, and headache without neck stiffness can still represent bacterial meningitis — particularly in early or partially treated cases.

features.evidenceLabel: Acute confusion or delirium with fever and headache — reflects meningoencephalitis or cerebral oedema
features.citation: van de Beek D et al. NEJM 2006. Altered mental status (confusion, disorientation, delirium, agitation) is present in ~70% of bacterial meningitis at diagnosis. It reflects meningoencephalitis, cerebral oedema, SIADH hyponatraemia, or hypoglycaemia. Acute confusion in the context of fever and headache carries a high prior probability for bacterial meningitis and mandates emergency evaluation.

features.evidenceLabel: GCS ≤12 at presentation — severe meningitis indicator; independent prognostic marker
features.citation: van de Beek D et al. NEJM 2006; Miner JR et al. Ann Emerg Med 1993. GCS ≤12 at presentation is present in 14–33% of bacterial meningitis. It is the strongest independent prognostic marker for adverse outcome (death or disability). A depressed GCS with fever and headache demands LP or empirical treatment without delay; CT first only if papilloedema or focal deficit present.

features.evidenceLabel: Cranial nerve palsies (CN III / VI raised ICP; CN VII / VIII meningococcal) — present in ~10–20%
features.citation: van de Beek D et al. NEJM 2006. Cranial nerve palsies occur in 10–20% of bacterial meningitis. CN III and VI palsy reflect raised intracranial pressure (false localising). CN VII (facial palsy) and CN VIII (sensorineural hearing loss) reflect direct inflammatory involvement of nerves in the subarachnoid space; Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae are the commonest causes.

features.evidenceLabel: Focal neurological signs — vasculitis, cerebral venous thrombosis, cerebral abscess, or herniation
features.citation: van de Beek D et al. NEJM 2006. Focal neurological deficits (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual field defects) occur in 20–30% of bacterial meningitis; they reflect septic arteritis, cortical venous thrombosis, subdural empyema, or transtentorial herniation. CT imaging before LP is mandatory when focal signs are present; empirical treatment must not be delayed pending imaging.

features.evidenceLabel: CSF pleocytosis with neutrophil (PMN) predominance — hallmark of bacterial over viral meningitis
features.citation: Spanos A et al. JAMA 1989. CSF neutrophil predominance (>80% PMN of total WCC) has a LR+ of 4.2 and LR− of 0.05 for bacterial vs viral meningitis. Bacterial meningitis typically shows 1000–10,000 WCC/µL with >80% neutrophils; viral aseptic meningitis shows lymphocyte predominance. Early bacterial meningitis may show lower cell counts but retains PMN predominance.

features.evidenceLabel: Positive blood cultures — near-definitive bacteraemia; yield 50–80% if drawn before antibiotics
features.citation: Tunkel AR et al. Clin Infect Dis 2004. Blood cultures yield the causative organism in 50–80% of bacterial meningitis when drawn before antibiotic administration. They are mandatory before LP and before empirical treatment; a 10-minute delay for blood cultures does not affect outcome, but they become negative within 15–30 min of effective antibiotic treatment. Positive blood cultures with meningeal symptoms are definitive.

features.evidenceLabel: CRP >100 mg/L — strongly supports bacterial over viral aetiology (LR+ ~4.8)
features.citation: Viallon A et al. Eur J Emerg Med 2011. CRP >100 mg/L has LR+ 4.8 and LR− 0.22 for bacterial vs viral meningitis. In combination with CSF parameters and procalcitonin, CRP contributes to the Bacterial Meningitis Score. A CRP <10 mg/L argues strongly against bacterial meningitis in an immunocompetent adult (LR− 0.06 for CSF pleocytosis + CRP <10).

features.evidenceLabel: LP opening pressure >25 cmH₂O — raised ICP present in majority of bacterial meningitis
features.citation: Tunkel AR et al. Clin Infect Dis 2004. CSF opening pressure is elevated (>25 cmH₂O) in the majority of bacterial meningitis cases; pressures >40 cmH₂O indicate severe raised ICP and risk of herniation. Monitoring and managing ICP (head elevation, osmotherapy, dexamethasone) is part of the management protocol. Extremely high opening pressure (>50 cmH₂O) is an indication for ICP monitoring.

features.evidenceLabel: Peripheral blood neutrophilia (WBC >15 × 10⁹/L with neutrophil predominance) — systemic bacterial sepsis
features.citation: van de Beek D et al. NEJM 2006. Peripheral neutrophilia is present in the majority of bacterial meningitis cases and reflects the systemic bacterial sepsis response. In combination with CRP and procalcitonin, it contributes to severity scoring. Leukopenia in the context of meningitis is an ominous sign suggesting Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (meningococcal septicaemia) or overwhelming sepsis.

features.evidenceLabel: Hyponatraemia (Na <135 mmol/L) — SIADH or cerebral salt wasting complication; worsens cerebral oedema
features.citation: Hasan I & Rashid T. Eur J Intern Med 2012. Hyponatraemia occurs in 30–60% of bacterial meningitis, from SIADH or cerebral salt wasting. It directly worsens cerebral oedema and contributes to altered consciousness and seizures. Fluid restriction (SIADH) vs isotonic saline replacement (CSW) are different management strategies. Hyponatraemia with meningitis is a marker of severity.

features.evidenceLabel: CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis (>50% lymphocytes) — viral / TB / cryptococcal / autoimmune pattern
features.citation: Spanos A et al. JAMA 1989. Lymphocyte predominance in CSF (>50% of pleocytosis) strongly favours viral aseptic meningitis (enterovirus, HSV, VZV), TB meningitis, or cryptococcal meningitis over bacterial aetiology. LR− for bacterial meningitis = 0.08 when CSF is lymphocytic. Early bacterial meningitis may be lymphocytic but this is uncommon; lymphocytic CSF substantially reduces bacterial probability.

features.evidenceLabel: Insidious onset over weeks — strongly suggests TB meningitis, cryptococcal, or carcinomatous meningitis
features.citation: Thwaites GE et al. NEJM 2004. Tuberculous meningitis classically presents with a 1–6 week prodrome of headache, malaise, low-grade fever, and meningism. An insidious onset over weeks substantially reduces bacterial meningitis probability and should prompt consideration of TB meningitis (India ink, AFB, Lowenstein-Jensen culture, ADA), cryptococcal meningitis (India ink, CrAg), and malignant meningitis.

features.evidenceLabel: Recent antibiotic treatment in preceding 48h — partially treated meningitis; may normalise CSF and cultures
features.citation: Kanegaye JT et al. Pediatrics 2001. Prior antibiotic treatment partially sterilises CSF and normalises cell counts and chemistry within 24–48h. Blood and CSF cultures may be negative in partially treated meningitis; CSF Gram stain becomes negative within 4–6h of antibiotic therapy. PCR retains sensitivity after partial treatment. A recent antibiotic course in a patient with persisting headache and fever warrants LP regardless.

features.evidenceLabel: Distinct viral prodrome (myalgia, sore throat, rash, coryza) days before meningism — favours viral aetiology
features.citation: Logan SAE & MacMahon E. BMJ 2008. A preceding viral prodrome of 3–7 days (myalgia, pharyngitis, coryzal symptoms, viral exanthem) before the onset of meningism argues for viral aseptic meningitis (enteroviral in summer/autumn, herpetic in any season). Bacterial meningitis typically presents acutely over hours with fewer prodromal symptoms. A clear viral prodrome reduces bacterial probability but does not exclude it.
Salvarani C et al. Ann Intern Med 2002. Age >50 required; mean 72y
Smetana GW. JAMA 2002. Jaw claudication LR+ 4.2; temporal tenderness LR+ 2.6
Smetana GW. JAMA 2002. Jaw claudication LR+ 4.2 (2.8–6.2) for positive biopsy

features.evidenceLabel: Visual loss / amaurosis fugax — RED FLAG
Tender / nodular temporal artery on palpation
Absent / reduced temporal artery pulse on palpation — ischaemic wall thickening
features.citation: Smetana GW & Shmerling RH. Arch Intern Med 2002. Absent temporal artery pulse LR+ 4.7 for GCA. Combined with beaded/tender artery: LR+ 9.0. Most specific bedside sign alongside jaw claudication.

features.evidenceLabel: Beaded or nodular temporal artery — granulomatous wall thickening
features.citation: Smetana GW & Shmerling RH. Arch Intern Med 2002. Beaded/prominent temporal artery LR+ 4.6; when combined with absent pulse, LR+ 9.0 for positive biopsy. Run finger along full temporal artery course.

features.evidenceLabel: Diplopia — oculomotor palsy from ophthalmic / posterior ciliary artery involvement
features.citation: Hayreh SS et al. Ophthalmology 1998. Diplopia in 6–15% of GCA; reflects ischaemia to extraocular muscles or III/IV/VI cranial nerve supply. Precedes permanent visual loss in some patients.

features.evidenceLabel: Scalp necrosis — ischaemic infarction from superficial temporal artery occlusion
features.citation: Ting JY et al. JAMA Dermatol 2014. Scalp necrosis is rare (<4%) but nearly pathognomonic for GCA; indicates complete vessel occlusion. Mandates immediate high-dose corticosteroids — delay risks further ischaemia.

features.evidenceLabel: Tongue pain / claudication on chewing or speaking — facial / lingual artery ischaemia
features.citation: Borg FA & Dasgupta B. Rheumatology 2009. Tongue or facial claudication in 6% of GCA; highly specific. Results from internal maxillary / lingual artery involvement. Risk of tongue infarction if untreated.

features.evidenceLabel: Fever, weight loss, fatigue — systemic inflammatory features
features.citation: Salvarani C et al. Ann Intern Med 2002. Constitutional symptoms (fever ≥37.5°C, weight loss, fatigue) present in 40–50% of GCA. Low-grade fever is more common than high fever; night sweats may occur.

features.evidenceLabel: Polymyalgia rheumatica — bilateral proximal girdle aching and morning stiffness
features.citation: Salvarani C & Hunder GG. Arthritis Rheum 2001. PMR coexists in 40–50% of GCA; presents with bilateral shoulder / hip girdle pain, morning stiffness >45 min. Some patients present with PMR first, then develop GCA.

features.evidenceLabel: Morning stiffness >45 minutes — PMR component or systemic inflammation
features.citation: Bird HA et al. Ann Rheum Dis 1979. Morning stiffness >45 min is one of the Jones criteria for PMR. When present with new headache in over-50, should raise GCA probability and prompt ESR/CRP.

features.evidenceLabel: New-onset headache in a patient over 50 — any new headache in this age group warrants GCA exclusion
features.citation: ACR/EULAR GCA Classification Criteria 2022. New headache of any type in patients >50y is one of the five ACR criteria. Prevalence of GCA increases sharply after age 70 (peak 70–80y).

features.evidenceLabel: Female sex — GCA predominates in women (F:M ratio 3:1)
features.citation: Lawrence RC et al. Arthritis Rheum 1998. GCA incidence: women 18.8/100,000/year vs men 6.9/100,000/year. Hormonal and genetic factors implicated; HLA-DRB1*04 alleles associated.

features.evidenceLabel: Northern European / Scandinavian ethnicity — highest GCA incidence worldwide
features.citation: Gonzalez-Gay MA et al. Semin Arthritis Rheum 2001. Incidence in Scandinavia 20–30/100,000/>50y; rare in Asian and African populations (<2/100,000). HLA class II allele frequency differences explain geographic variation.

features.evidenceLabel: ESR >50 mm/h (mean 90–100 mm/h in GCA) — markedly elevated
features.citation: Smetana GW & Shmerling RH. Arch Intern Med 2002. ESR >50 mm/h LR+ 1.2 (low discriminating value alone); ESR >47 sensitivity 84%, specificity 56%. Most patients >70 mm/h. ESR normal in <4% — near-exclusion.

features.evidenceLabel: Temporal artery ultrasound — hypoechoic halo sign (vessel wall oedema)
features.citation: Karassa FB et al. Ann Intern Med 2005. Halo sign sensitivity 69%, specificity 82%, LR+ 3.9. EULAR recommends ultrasound as first-line imaging; halo sign may disappear after 1–2 weeks of steroids — scan urgently.

features.evidenceLabel: PET-CT — FDG uptake in aorta / subclavian / axillary arteries (large vessel GCA)
features.citation: Blockmans D et al. Ann Rheum Dis 2006. PET-CT sensitivity 80% for large vessel GCA; identifies aortitis (40%) and subclavian involvement. Large vessel GCA carries higher risk of aortic aneurysm.
Foroozan R et al. Ophthalmology 2002. Thrombocytosis present in ~50% of biopsy-proven GCA; reflects IL-6-driven thrombopoietin stimulation. Useful supportive finding when ESR/CRP inconclusive.

features.evidenceLabel: Normochromic normocytic anaemia — anaemia of chronic inflammation
features.citation: Salvarani C et al. Ann Intern Med 2002. Anaemia in 25–50% of GCA; normochromic normocytic pattern from IL-6–mediated suppression of erythropoiesis. Hb typically 100–120 g/L.

features.evidenceLabel: Age under 50 — GCA almost never occurs below age 50 (case reports only)
features.citation: Salvarani C et al. Ann Intern Med 2002. Fewer than 2% of biopsy-proven GCA cases occur in patients <50 years. Age under 50 is a near-absolute exclusion criterion for GCA.

features.evidenceLabel: Normal ESR (<20 mm/h) AND normal CRP — near-excludes active GCA
features.citation: Hayreh SS et al. Graefes Arch Clin Exp Ophthalmol 1997. Normal ESR and CRP together have LR- 0.04 for GCA. <4% of confirmed GCA has normal inflammatory markers; if both normal, alternative diagnosis strongly favoured.

features.evidenceLabel: Normal temporal arteries bilaterally — no tenderness, pulse present, not nodular
features.citation: Smetana GW & Shmerling RH. Arch Intern Med 2002. Absence of any temporal artery abnormality reduces post-test probability. However, normal exam does not exclude GCA — biopsy required if clinical suspicion remains.

features.evidenceLabel: Scintillating scotoma — expanding arc of shimmering zigzag (fortification spectra)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Scintillating scotoma is pathognomonic for migraine aura; no other primary headache produces this phenomenon. Expands centrifugally from paracentral fixation over 20–30 min.

features.evidenceLabel: Aura symptoms spread gradually over ≥5 minutes — key ICHD-3 criterion distinguishing from TIA
features.citation: Fisher CM. Headache 1986. Gradual spread (march) of visual or sensory aura is the cardinal feature distinguishing migraine from TIA. TIA symptoms are sudden-onset maximal; migraine aura evolves slowly over 5–30 min.

features.evidenceLabel: Aura duration 5–60 minutes — fully reversible within 1 hour
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Each aura symptom must last 5–60 min; if multiple aura types, total duration up to 60 min per symptom. Duration >60 min raises concern for TIA (especially if age >50 or cardiovascular risk factors present).

features.evidenceLabel: Unilateral pulsating headache follows or accompanies aura within 60 minutes
