features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Headache within 60 min of aura onset is a diagnostic criterion. Headache may precede, accompany, or follow the aura phase. 'Acephalgic migraine' (aura without headache) is a recognised subtype.

features.evidenceLabel: Positive visual phenomena — phosphenes, flashes, geometric patterns
features.citation: Headache Classification Committee. Cephalalgia 2018. Positive aura symptoms (flickering lights, stars, geometric shapes) reflect cortical spreading depolarisation propagating across visual cortex at 3–5 mm/min.

features.evidenceLabel: Negative visual phenomena — scotoma, visual field defect, blurred vision
features.citation: Cutrer FM & Huerter K. Neurologist 2007. Negative symptoms (scotoma, loss of vision) represent cortical depression after spreading depolarisation. Homonymous distribution reflects involvement of posterior visual cortex.

features.evidenceLabel: Unilateral sensory aura — spreading tingling / numbness (cheiro-oral distribution)
features.citation: Russell MB & Olesen J. Brain 1996. Sensory aura in 31% of MwA; cheiro-oral (hand → face → mouth) spreading distribution reflects somatosensory cortex depolarisation. Distinguishes from TIA by gradual spread.

features.evidenceLabel: Dysphasic aura — speech difficulties (word-finding, paraphasias) during aura
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Speech/language disturbance in 17–20% of MwA; usually expressive dysphasia. Fully reversible. When isolated without other aura features in age >50, TIA exclusion is mandatory.

features.evidenceLabel: Unilateral motor weakness (hemiplegic migraine) — fully reversible motor aura
features.citation: Thomsen LL et al. Brain 2002. Familial (FHM) and sporadic hemiplegic migraine. CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A gene mutations in familial form. Motor aura lasts up to 72h; mandates TIA/stroke exclusion on first presentation.

features.evidenceLabel: Unilateral headache following aura (typically ipsilateral to contralateral aura)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Headache is unilateral in 60–70% of MwA; may be contralateral or ipsilateral to the aura. Side-locked headache should prompt secondary cause workup.

features.evidenceLabel: Pulsating / throbbing headache following aura phase
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Pulsating quality is one of the four headache criteria; present in >50% of MwA attacks. Reflects trigeminovascular activation and vasoactive peptide release following cortical spreading depression.

features.evidenceLabel: Nausea and/or vomiting during headache phase
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Nausea/vomiting is a required associated symptom; present in 80–90% of attacks. May begin during aura phase before headache onset. Severe vomiting may require parenteral antiemetics.

features.evidenceLabel: Photophobia and phonophobia during headache phase
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Photophobia and phonophobia required in MwA headache criteria. Reflect central sensitisation of trigeminovascular pathways. Phonophobia (sound sensitivity) often the first reported associated symptom.

features.evidenceLabel: Headache aggravated by routine physical activity (walking, stairs)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Aggravation by physical activity is one of the four headache criteria. Reflects pulsatile component of pain; vasodilation theory partially supported but trigeminovascular model now predominant.

features.evidenceLabel: Personal history of confirmed migraine with aura
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. At least five attacks fulfilling criteria required for MwA diagnosis. In known MwA patient, recurrent typical attack in same pattern has very high positive predictive value.

features.evidenceLabel: Family history of migraine with aura — heritability 50–65%
features.citation: Mulder EJ et al. Cephalalgia 2003. Heritability of MwA 65% (higher than MwOA 45%). Familial hemiplegic migraine is autosomal dominant with single gene mutations identified (CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A).

features.evidenceLabel: OCP use in MwA — combined OCP is WHO MEC Category 4 (contraindicated) due to stroke risk
features.citation: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria 2015. MwA + COC: OR 8–13 for ischaemic stroke. MwOA + COC: OR 2. OCP should be discontinued and alternative contraception offered. Progestogen-only acceptable.

features.evidenceLabel: Aura of sudden maximal onset (not gradual) — argues for TIA over migraine aura
features.citation: Fisher CM. Headache 1986. Abrupt-onset visual or sensory symptoms without spread are more characteristic of TIA than migraine aura. The spreading march of aura is the key differentiating feature.

features.evidenceLabel: Aura lasting >60 minutes without resolution — raises concern for TIA / CVST / AVM
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Aura >60 min is defined as prolonged aura; onset >50y with first aura >60 min mandates TIA exclusion. Consider carotid imaging and cardiac workup. CVST can mimic prolonged aura.

features.evidenceLabel: Aura without subsequent headache — acephalgic migraine or consider TIA in age >50
features.citation: Fisher CM. Trans Am Neurol Assoc 1980. Acephalgic migraine (aura without headache) is a recognised ICHD-3 subtype (1.2.3). In patients >50y with new-onset aura-like symptoms without headache, TIA investigation required.

features.evidenceLabel: New-onset aura-type symptoms after age 50 — TIA must be excluded before diagnosing MwA
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. New-onset visual/sensory symptoms in age >50 without prior migraine history requires TIA workup (MRI DWI, carotid duplex, ECG, echocardiogram) before migraine diagnosis. Prior migraine history essential context.

features.evidenceLabel: Identical / stereotyped aura with every attack — single strongest discriminator from TIA
features.citation: Fisher CM. Headache 1986; Olesen J et al. Cephalalgia 2004. A stereotyped, reproducible aura pattern (same visual phenomena, same spread, same duration attack after attack over years) is the single strongest discriminator between MwA and TIA. TIA produces variable deficits reflecting different ischaemic territories each time; migraine aura is generated by cortical spreading depression and recapitulates the same cortical pathway reliably.

features.evidenceLabel: Aura spreads sequentially across modalities (visual → sensory → speech) over minutes
features.citation: Fisher CM. Headache 1986. Migration of aura across modalities in sequence — visual phenomena first, then spreading tingling from hand to face (cheiro-oral march), then speech difficulty — over 20–40 minutes is characteristic of cortical spreading depression. TIA produces simultaneous multi-territory deficits reflecting embolic occlusion, not sequential spread. Sequential march is highly discriminating (LR+ ~8).

features.evidenceLabel: Sensory aura spreading from hand to face (cheiro-oral march) — somatotopic cortical spread
features.citation: Fisher CM. Headache 1986. The cheiro-oral march — tingling beginning in the fingers, spreading up the arm and across to the face over 10–20 minutes — reflects the somatotopic organisation of the somatosensory cortex and the slow (3 mm/min) propagation of cortical spreading depression. This march pattern is pathognomonic for cortical origin and strongly argues against TIA.

features.evidenceLabel: Brainstem aura — vertigo, diplopia, tinnitus, dysarthria, bilateral paraesthesia (ICHD-3 distinct subtype)
features.citation: ICHD-3 2018. Migraine with brainstem aura (formerly basilar-type migraine) includes at least 2 of: dysarthria, vertigo, tinnitus, hypacusis, diplopia, ataxia, or decreased level of consciousness — all fully reversible. ICHD-3 now requires these without motor weakness. Recognition is clinically important because brainstem aura mimics vertebrobasilar TIA and can trigger unnecessary anticoagulation.

features.evidenceLabel: Classic fortification spectra — zigzag arc of luminous angles expanding peripherally over 20–30 min
features.citation: Richards W. Sci Am 1971; Wilkinson F. Cephalalgia 2004. Fortification spectra (teichopsia) — an expanding arc of angular, shimmering zigzag lines that begins as a blind spot near fixation and migrates to the peripheral field over 20–30 minutes — represents cortical spreading depression crossing the calcarine cortex. This specific morphology is near-pathognomonic for migraine; TIA does not produce this expanding crescent pattern.

features.evidenceLabel: Triptan reliably aborts the headache phase (not the aura) — confirms migrainous mechanism
features.citation: Tfelt-Hansen PC et al. Cephalalgia 2000. Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists that abort the headache phase of MwA; they do not shorten the aura (which is driven by cortical spreading depression, not trigeminal activation). Consistent triptan response for the headache phase while aura runs its course confirms the biphasic MwA mechanism and supports the diagnosis.

features.evidenceLabel: Response to migraine preventive therapy — topiramate, valproate, beta-blocker, amitriptyline, CGRP mAb
features.citation: Silberstein SD et al. Neurology 2012 (evidence review). Response to evidence-based migraine preventives (topiramate 100 mg, valproate 500–1500 mg, propranolol 40–240 mg, amitriptyline 25–75 mg, or anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies) with ≥50% reduction in attack frequency is a strong positive marker for migraine diagnosis. These agents are ineffective for TIA and most other headache disorders.

features.evidenceLabel: Seeks dark, quiet room during headache phase — photophobia + phonophobia driving behaviour
features.citation: Goadsby PJ et al. NEJM 2002. The compulsion to lie in a dark, quiet room is among the most clinically reliable features of migraine. It is driven by ictal photophobia (thalamic sensitisation to light via the retino-thalamo-cortical pathway) and phonophobia. This withdrawal behaviour is absent in TIA (which causes no pain or photophobia) and less characteristic of TTH.

features.value: Normal MRI DWI during / after aura
features.evidenceLabel: Normal MRI DWI (no acute ischaemia) obtained during or within 24h of aura — confirms migraine not TIA
features.citation: Ay H et al. Neurology 2006. DWI MRI detects acute ischaemic stroke within minutes; TIA with DWI lesion (40–67% of TIAs) or subsequent stroke confirms ischaemic aetiology. Normal DWI during or immediately after focal neurological symptoms argues strongly for migraine aura over TIA. This is the key investigation when the aura-TIA distinction cannot be made clinically.

features.evidenceLabel: Normal carotid duplex or CTA — no significant stenosis or dissection; reduces TIA probability
features.citation: Johnston SC et al. Lancet Neurol 2007. Carotid artery disease (stenosis >50%, dissection) is a major TIA/stroke risk factor. Normal carotid imaging combined with typical MwA features substantially reduces the probability of embolic TIA. A negative vascular workup (carotid Doppler + echo + Holter) in a young female with classic stereotyped aura effectively confirms primary MwA.

features.evidenceLabel: Female sex — 3:1 F:M prevalence ratio in migraine with aura
features.citation: Lipton RB et al. Headache 2001. Migraine with aura has a female predominance of approximately 3:1 (F:M); prevalence 18% women vs 6% men in reproductive age. The female predominance is related to oestrogen-mediated cortical excitability and lower threshold for cortical spreading depression. Hormonal influences are particularly pronounced in MwA (menstrual migraine, OCP sensitivity).

features.evidenceLabel: Premonitory / prodrome symptoms hours before aura (yawning, fatigue, food craving, mood change)
features.citation: Giffin NJ et al. Neurology 2003. Prodromal symptoms (yawning 36%, fatigue 23%, mood change 17%, food craving 15%) precede migraine aura by 2–48 hours; they reflect hypothalamic/dopaminergic activation before cortical spreading depression. Recognition of the prodrome in MwA is clinically important as it extends the window for preventive intervention before aura onset.

features.evidenceLabel: Postdrome phase — cognitive fog, fatigue, neck stiffness, difficulty concentrating after headache resolves
features.citation: Giffin NJ et al. Neurology 2003; Kelman L & Rains JC. Headache 2005. A postdrome phase lasting 4–48 hours (cognitive fog, fatigue, mood change, scalp tenderness, neck stiffness) follows the headache in ~80% of migraineurs. The postdrome phase has no parallel in TIA or secondary headache and, when reported by the patient, is a strong positive marker for primary migraine.

features.evidenceLabel: Simultaneous onset of deficits in multiple non-contiguous territories — TIA pattern, not migraine
features.citation: Fisher CM. Headache 1986. Migraine aura spreads slowly and sequentially (cortical spreading depression; 3 mm/min). TIA produces simultaneous deficits in multiple territories reflecting embolic or haemodynamic ischaemia. Simultaneous onset of, e.g., visual field loss AND contralateral weakness AND speech loss — without sequential spread — strongly favours TIA over MwA and warrants emergency vascular evaluation.

features.evidenceLabel: Known atrial fibrillation — cardioembolic source shifts diagnosis strongly toward TIA over migraine aura
features.citation: Johnston SC et al. Lancet Neurol 2007. AF is the most common identifiable cardioembolic source for TIA/stroke; it carries an annual stroke risk of 1–5% uninanticoagulated. Any focal neurological episode in a patient with AF must be treated as TIA until proven otherwise. The combination of AF + focal neurological symptoms is a clinical emergency; migraine aura as the explanation requires exclusion of embolism first.

features.evidenceLabel: Known ≥50% ipsilateral carotid stenosis or recent dissection — high TIA/stroke probability
features.citation: Rothwell PM et al. Lancet 2007 (NASCET/ECST). Symptomatic carotid stenosis ≥50% carries an ipsilateral stroke risk of ~15% at 2 years uninrevascularised. Any new focal neurological episode ipsilateral to a significant stenosis or recent dissection should be investigated as TIA first. Migraine aura is a diagnosis of exclusion in this context.

features.evidenceLabel: Pure isolated motor weakness without positive sensory or visual phenomena — TIA pattern not migraine
features.citation: Fisher CM. Headache 1986; ICHD-3 2018. Migraine aura characteristically includes positive phenomena (tingling, flashing lights, zigzag) arising from spreading cortical activation before the negative (deficit) phase. Pure isolated motor deficit without any positive sensory or visual features is atypical for MwA and more consistent with capsular or subcortical TIA. Hemiplegic migraine is a specific ICHD-3 entity requiring family history or genetic confirmation.
